frameworks.name: The Circumplex Check
frameworks.summary: A two-minute pre-meeting calibration that places the room's need and your default behaviour on the dominance and warmth axes, so you can adjust the one axis that is actually wrong.
steps: Write your default behaviour in one line - how you behave when you are not managing yourself, using a scale from 'warm and accommodating' to 'cold and controlling'.
Write the room's requirement in one line - what the situation needs from you, in the same two dimensions.
Plot both on the two axes and identify the single axis where the gap is largest. Only one axis is usually wrong.

Diagnose the failure mode: if you are too dominant, the cost is suppressed bad news; if you are too warm, the cost is no decision; if you are too cold, the cost is no candour; if you are too submissive, the cost is no leadership.
Choose the smallest adjustment that closes the gap - one change in volume, pace, question density, or warmth of framing - and hold it for the first three minutes.
Re-check at the halfway point using the question-quality test: are they asking sharper questions than they were, or fewer?
frameworks.whenToUse: Before any meeting where your position or your standing is at stake. Skip it for routine updates, and skip it for genuine crises, where the decision matters more than the calibration.
frameworks.example: A founder arrives at a board meeting needing a runway extension. Her default is warm and accommodating; the room's requirement is dominant and cold, because a board run without a strong proposal defaults to cutting spend. The gap is on dominance only. She therefore does not soften her delivery - she hardens the framing: the number first, the ask second, and she takes the first three minutes without softening or hedging. The room responds to the structure, not to the emotion.

frameworks.name: The Room Temperature Read
frameworks.summary: A fast, tiered scan of a live room that converts observable signals into one named reading and one prepared move.
steps: Set a cadence: scan every three to five minutes, at a fixed point in the conversation, so the read becomes routine rather than anxiety.
Read tier one only first - body orientation, phone use, note-taking, overlap pattern, and the quality of the last question asked.
Name the temperature in one word - cold, guarded, neutral, warm, or hot - and name the evidence that produced it.
Identify the cause from four possibilities: unclear content, missing stakes, unresolved opposition, or a failure of the senior person in the room to set the frame.
Attach one prepared move per cause: clarify the decision, sharpen the stake, name the trade-off, or hand the floor to the senior person.
Execute the move and re-scan after three minutes; if the reading has not changed, escalate to a different cause rather than repeating the move.
frameworks.whenToUse: Any time you are presenting, and periodically in any meeting you are running. Do not use it in one-to-ones, where the signals are far richer and the read takes seconds.
frameworks.example: At minute 14 of a Series B update, three people are on their phones, nobody has asked a question since minute 4, and the CFO is leaning back. The read is cold, cause number one: unclear content. The move is a decision question - 'Which of these three numbers should I spend the next ten minutes on?' The room re-engages because the choice transfers work back to them.

frameworks.name: The 5-Minute Reset
frameworks.summary: A five-part, timed intervention that changes a cold or hostile room's question type, physical state, participation structure, and decision state without ending the meeting.
steps: 0:00-0:45 - Change the question type, not your tone: move from evaluate to imagine, or from argue to specify.
0:45-1:30 - Change the physical state: stand, move, put the laptop down, change the slide, offer water.
1:30-2:30 - Ask one real question, then be silent for a full five seconds.
2:30-3:30 - Change the participation structure: hand the floor to someone who has not spoken, and if you are senior, hand it explicitly.
3:30-4:30 - Name the trade-off in front of the room as a priced choice.
4:30-5:00 - Close on a decision or a named next move, and state it aloud.
frameworks.whenToUse: When the room has gone cold, gone flat, or turned openly hostile and the meeting still has to produce a decision. Do not use it when a live clock is running, and do not use it as a substitute for a decision you are entitled to make.
frameworks.example: Forty minutes into a strategy review, the room has turned into a slow argument between two directors and the CEO has said nothing for fifteen minutes. The junior facilitator changes the question type to 'what would have to be true for the opposite to be right', moves to the whiteboard, asks the ops lead what breaks first operationally, and closes by naming the trade-off and assigning a one-week test.

frameworks.name: The Status Cue Audit
frameworks.summary: A deliberate, one-week audit of how status is signalled in your organisation, designed to find the status games you play and the ones you have learned to read.
steps: List the status cues your organisation uses: speaking order, interruption patterns, who gets asked, who is interrupted, address conventions, seating, and artefact handling.
Mark each cue as legitimate (it tracks actual contribution or responsibility) or game (it signals rank without doing work).
Audit your own behaviour against the game list, and pick the one game you play most - usually the most costly to your credibility.
Replace that game with a legitimate equivalent: credit publicly, hold ground on facts, arrive prepared, ask the unlocking question.
Audit the room: identify the senior person in the room by observation, and note where the formal hierarchy and the behavioural hierarchy disagree - that gap is where your influence is highest.
Set a personal rule for what you will not do to signal rank, and one measurable behaviour that will replace it, then check it in a recorded meeting.
frameworks.whenToUse: Once per quarter, and immediately after a promotion, a new role, or joining a new company. Also run it before a major interview or a high-stakes investor or board event, where the room's cue system will be unfamiliar.
frameworks.example: An audit reveals three games in the company: interrupting to be first, name-dropping senior people to borrow their status, and using a shared 'how hard are you working' metric in place of a real one. The executive replaces the name-dropping with a public credit habit, and the metric game with a written decision log - and the room's response is to start bringing him real problems earlier, which is the entire point.

scenarios.title: The board meeting where the CFO disagrees with you, in front of the board
scenarios.setting: Quarterly board meeting, eight people, you are presenting a pricing change that raises churn risk. The CFO, a founder-level operator of 14 years' tenure, says publicly: 'I don't think this is a pricing change, it's a revenue miss in disguise.'
scenarios.challenge: The board turns to you. Every instinct says defend the model with the full dataset. The CFO is more senior than you in the room's eyes and he is not wrong that churn is a risk.
objectives: Hold credibility without a public contest
Convert a personal challenge into a board-level decision
Leave the board with a clear next move

options.text: Defend immediately and at length: walk through the full elasticity model, the cohort data, and the three ways churn is controlled.
options.outcome: You speak for four minutes against a room that has already formed a view. The CFO appears gracious in conceding, and the board's private conclusion is that you cannot hold a disagreement with a peer - which matters far more than the pricing decision.
options.feedback: Defending at length against the first challenge converts a proposal into a contest about you, and the room resolves it in whichever direction requires less work. Acknowledge the risk in the CFO's own framing, then move to the trade-off - what the board must give up to buy the churn reduction - and let the board decide. The board wants to see you handle this, not win it.

options.text: Defend with data but in a measured way: 'That is the right concern. Here is the number I think has not been shared yet - 6.2 percent of enterprise accounts would churn, which is X dollars against Y dollars of new ARR. Which of those two numbers do you want to spend the next ten minutes on?'
options.outcome: The room reframes from 'whose analysis is right' to 'which number matters'. You have not won the point and you have not lost it, and the board is now working rather than watching a duel. The CFO is still the perceived authority, which is acceptable for this meeting.
options.feedback: This is close to the right move: acknowledge, supply the missing fact, and hand back a decision about where to spend attention. Tighten it by naming the trade-off explicitly - what the board gives up if it takes the churn hit - because a room that is given a real choice stops defending and starts deciding. Also keep the number short: one figure, not three.

options.text: Concede immediately: 'You're right, let's hold the pricing change and revisit next quarter.'
options.outcome: The meeting moves on and you have preserved the relationship with the CFO. You have also taught the board that your proposals can be withdrawn by a single objection, and the pricing change you had modelled for three months is dead without a test.
options.feedback: This is a retreat presented as deference, and the board will read it as weakness rather than as wisdom. If you genuinely think the change should be held, propose the test - a limited rollout to new enterprise accounts, with a six-week checkpoint - so that conceding on the decision still produces movement on the substance.

options.text: Reframe to the room as a shared problem: 'Let me put the trade-off on the table rather than defend a number. We are choosing between price and retention, and the honest version of that is that we can have one in the first quarter. If we take the pricing change, we should expect roughly 6 percent enterprise churn and plan the retention spend now. If we hold pricing, we should plan the revenue gap now. Which do you want to plan against?'
options.outcome: The disagreement stops being a contest between you and the CFO and becomes a board decision with two priced options. The CFO has to contribute rather than just object, and the board gets to decide rather than adjudicate. The price: you must accept a decision you might lose.
options.feedback: This is the target behaviour. It names the trade-off, prices both branches, and moves the decision to where authority actually lives. Two refinements: name the trade-off earlier - before the CFO has framed it as a character issue - and explicitly invite the CFO's contribution to the retention plan, so the board sees collaboration rather than surrender.

scenarios.coachingNote: A public challenge in a senior room is a test of your frame, not your dataset. Acknowledge, reframe the disagreement into a shared trade-off, price both branches, and hand the decision to the room. The person who loses a decision but keeps the room's trust has done it right.

scenarios.title: The pitch where the room is on its phones
scenarios.setting: Series A investor meeting, four partners, you have 12 minutes. Two partners have been looking at their phones for the last four minutes, and one has started checking the time.
scenarios.challenge: You are 60 percent through a well-rehearsed deck, and the room has stopped being present. Continuing the script will lose the meeting.
objectives: Diagnose whether disengagement is content, delivery, or context
Recover attention without pleading
Get a specific next step out of the room

options.text: Speed up and add energy, as if the room were a stadium.
options.outcome: The pace climbs, the room does not re-engage, and the partners experience the change as pressure rather than energy. You have now signalled that you noticed, which is a loss of composure in front of four people who will describe you to their partners later.
options.feedback: Energy is a response to a warm room, not a mechanism for reviving a cold one. Raising volume when attention is gone reads as anxiety and often accelerates disengagement. Diagnose first - is it the content, the delivery, or a meeting that is running long in a bad slot?

options.text: Pause, look at the room, and ask: 'I want to make sure I'm using your time well - which of the last three slides deserves the next ten minutes?'
options.outcome: The question hands the room work and forces an explicit answer. You have learned something real about the content they care about, and you have recovered the floor without pleading - but the two partners on their phones may still be gone, because the question addressed the room's engagement, not its attention.
options.feedback: A reasonable move with one flaw: it treats disengagement as a shared decision when it is not. Make the question sharper by naming the specific cost of the next ten minutes: 'I have eight minutes of product roadmap left. If you would rather spend those on unit economics, say so and I will move on.' Concrete time and a real choice recover attention better than an open-ended check-in.

options.text: Stop the deck entirely, put a number on the screen, and say: 'Let me skip to the one thing you actually need: we closed 14 enterprise accounts last quarter at 2.1 percent of the base. I will spend six minutes there and then you can decide whether to continue.'
options.outcome: You have demonstrated control by cutting your own material, which is itself a status and credibility signal. The room now has a short, concrete agenda and a clear exit. The risk: you have conceded the frame before you know whether the partners wanted product or economics.
options.feedback: Strong move - cutting your own deck is a legitimate power move that reads as confidence rather than as capitulation. Tighten it by asking the question you are really asking: 'Is there anything on the agenda you want me to skip so we can get to the decision?' That gets you the information while keeping the frame, and it stops the meeting from becoming a referendum on your deck rather than on your business.

options.text: Keep going and assume they are just taking notes, then close by asking for a specific commitment: 'Before we finish - what would have to be true for you to lead this round?'
options.outcome: You get a clean, high-quality close. The partners also get a clean read that you did not notice two of them were out for the last six minutes - which suggests you are either oblivious to the room or that you noticed and did nothing.
options.feedback: This is the most common and most damaging failure: treating disengagement as a reading problem rather than a performance problem. It risks the relationship, and a partner who was checking their phone is a partner who is now deciding whether to take the meeting internally. Read the room, name the cost of the next ten minutes, and give them a real choice about what to skip.

scenarios.coachingNote: Attention is the currency of the room and you spend it whether or not you notice. When a room is gone, the recovery is not effort - it is evidence of control: cut your own material, name the time cost, and offer a specific alternative.

scenarios.title: The all-hands where you are the least senior presenter on the agenda
scenarios.setting: Company all-hands, 1,800 people, in person. You are the newest director, presenting a project that two VPs are also presenting. The CEO is in the third row.
scenarios.challenge: Your project has real results. But the two VPs who present before you have ten years each, and the CEO is sitting in the front half of the room with a visible lack of interest in you.
objectives: Hold the room without competing on status
Make your results land in five minutes
Avoid the appearance of over-reach

options.text: Open by acknowledging the hierarchy directly: 'I know I'm newer than the people who spoke before me, so I want to be brief - here's what I learned, and here's what I'd like help with.'
options.outcome: The framing signals self-awareness and the CEO relaxes slightly. It also puts a ceiling on your own authority that you imposed, and the room now expects a junior contribution rather than a leader's message.
options.feedback: The humility is genuine and it helps, but the sentence is a status concession you did not have to make and the room notices the concession. You can convey the same thing by attributing clearly instead - name the two people whose work produced the result - which demonstrates hierarchy awareness without announcing your rank. Status cues in front of 1,800 people are expensive; a self-diminishing framing in an all-hands is a permanent artefact.

options.text: Lead with a specific result, attribute it to two named people, then ask the room one question that only a person with your role could ask.
options.outcome: You have demonstrated status the only way that transfers at scale: specificity plus generosity. The CEO's attention shifts from 'who is this person' to 'this is a result', and your question gives the room a role. The 1,800 people remember the names you gave credit to, not the hierarchy.
options.feedback: This is the target. Credit is the cheapest and most durable status signal, and naming specific people in front of a large audience is the one form of it that is unambiguously credible. Pair it with the discipline of naming a cost or a limit in your own result - 'this worked for segment X, and it will not work for segment Y' - because unqualified wins invite the room to discount you, and the CEO discount is the one that matters.

options.text: Mirror the VPs' format exactly - same slide template, same structure, same level of polish - and deliver the same kind of content.
options.outcome: You look like a smaller version of a senior person. The room gives you the same attention it gives the VPs, which is to say none, because you have signalled you are an imitation rather than a source.
options.feedback: Formatting is not strategy. Copying a senior person's delivery template tells the room where to file you. Choose the format that fits the one thing only you can say - the frontline number, the customer quote, the failure nobody else will admit to - and give that disproportionate time.

options.text: Skip your slides and tell a 90-second story about a customer who nearly churned, with the number attached at the end.
options.outcome: The story is memorable and the number lands. But the CEO, who is three rows in and will be asked afterwards whether the all-hands was worth the time, now has to remember what you did, and you have made that his problem.
options.feedback: The narrative instinct is right and stories beat slides in large rooms. The problem is that you have made yourself memorable rather than legible - a 1,800-person room cannot infer your role or your remit from a good story. Add one sentence establishing your remit before the story begins, so the audience knows why this person is talking, and the story does the rest.

scenarios.coachingNote: In a large room, status is transferred by attribution and specificity, not by volume. Name the people who made the result, name the limit of the result, and ask the one question only your role allows. That is how you hold a room you do not outrank.

scenarios.title: The strategy offsite where the room is cold and you cannot explain why
scenarios.setting: A two-day executive offsite, 11 people, offtsite in a lodge. You are facilitating. The morning session on 'long-term positioning' has produced three polite nods and no engagement for 50 minutes.
scenarios.challenge: The offsite is a two-day event with a facilitator budget of reputational capital. Something is wrong, and the room is not telling you what.
objectives: Determine whether the problem is content, process, or the offsite itself
Reset without blaming or apologising excessively
Extract a real decision from a dead session

options.text: Ask the room directly: 'I am getting nothing from this - what is wrong with this session?'
options.outcome: You get honest feedback, which is useful, and you have also told 11 executives that you cannot read the room - precisely the skill an offsite facilitator is hired for. The session is now about your facilitation.
options.feedback: Honest and probably necessary eventually, but the sequence is wrong - asking a room what is wrong with the room in front of the room makes the feedback about you. Diagnose privately first: ask two of the eleven for the real reason during the break. Then run a reset designed for the cause you find, rather than a general request for feedback that will produce polite non-answers in a group setting.

options.text: Assume the content is wrong and replace the entire morning block: 'Let us stop here. I want to change what we do with the rest of the morning - we will spend it on the three decisions we came here to make.'
options.outcome: The switch to decisions is the right instinct - decision work is more engaging than discussion work. But you have discarded 50 minutes of the offsite's agenda without explanation, and the CEO will ask why the schedule changed.
options.feedback: Moving to decisions is the strongest single move available and it is the right instinct, but make the change legible rather than abrupt. One sentence of framing protects you: 'I want to use the rest of the morning on the decisions rather than the framing, because we will not get the framing from a discussion.' Then, at the end of the day, tell the CEO what you observed and why you changed it - facilitators who explain their interventions in hindsight are trusted for the next one.

options.text: Break for 20 minutes, walk out, and in the break ask three people individually what is actually wrong.
options.outcome: You learn that the real problem is the hotel, or that the CEO's warning to the team the night before has everyone braced for bad news, or that two of the eleven are in an unresolved conflict. You can then reset with the actual cause. The room experiences a clean break.
options.feedback: This is the professional move: diagnose the cause privately, then intervene publicly with a fix that fits the cause. A 20-minute break is unremarkable in a two-day offsite, so it costs you nothing in authority. The discipline is not to skip the private diagnosis - a reset built on a guess is worse than no reset, because you will spend your one intervention on the wrong problem and have no second attempt.

options.text: Push harder on the content: bring in the customer research you did not have time to include, add the market data, and give the room a better case to react to.
options.outcome: You spend 40 minutes presenting. The room is still polite. The offsite now feels like it was about your preparation rather than about their company.
options.feedback: Adding content to an unresponsive room is the most common offsite failure and it almost never works - unresponsive rooms are rarely short of material, they are short of a reason to care. Notice also that you are the facilitator, so you are the least entitled person in the building to have a view. When the room has been unresponsive for 50 minutes, the subject is not the topic.

scenarios.coachingNote: A cold room is a diagnosis, not a delivery problem. Break privately, find the real cause among the people, and choose one intervention that fits it. The facilitator's job is not to hold the agenda; it is to hold the room.

scenarios.title: The customer call where the buyer outranks you and wants your opinion
scenarios.setting: A prospect call with a Fortune 500 procurement lead, an IT director, and their CEO. You are the founder of a 30-person vendor. The CEO says: 'We like you, but you have to convince my IT team. Talk to them like you talk to me.'
scenarios.challenge: The most senior person in the room has told you, explicitly, to talk down to the people he has put you in front of - and those people are the ones who will actually build or kill the deal.
objectives: Read the real power structure under an unusual instruction
Address the IT team in a way the CEO will not hear as insubordination
Advance the deal without a political misstep

options.text: Follow the instruction literally and speak mostly to the IT director, giving the technical detail the CEO has told you to skip.
options.outcome: The CEO is briefly satisfied. The IT director, who is now being managed, becomes the champion of your disqualification - and the CEO has handed you his attention, which is what he was actually testing.
options.feedback: This misreads the instruction. The CEO was not delegating a speaking task; he was establishing that he controls the room and probing how you handle the people below him. Obeying literally makes you politically naïve and hands the deal to the person with the veto. Address the IT director on substance, but keep your eye line and your framing on the CEO - the room is watching to see who you talk to.

options.text: Answer the CEO's challenge directly and warmly - 'I will absolutely talk to them properly, but I want to get one thing from you first, because you framed the problem for me' - then take the technical question to the IT team with the CEO visibly included in the answer.
options.outcome: The CEO's instruction is honoured in substance without the political error, the IT director gets a real answer, and the CEO looks like the sponsor rather than the absentee. The only risk is that a genuinely humble CEO reads your redirect as clever.
options.feedback: This handles the subordination trap correctly: you treat the instruction as a request for respect, not as permission to lose the room. The technique - honour the instruction's intent while redirecting the frame - is generalisable to any room where a senior person tries to put you in a subordinate position. Keep the warm tone, and make sure the IT director's technical question is answered substantively, not deferred.

options.text: Ignore the CEO entirely and treat the IT director as an equal, going straight to the architecture diagram and the security questionnaire.
options.outcome: The IT director warms to you considerably. The CEO checks his phone, and you have lost the only person in the room who can approve anything - whatever the IT director likes, procurement will now have to fight for it.
options.feedback: The substance is right and the politics are wrong. In a room with a clear hierarchy, the way you treat the most senior person is the signal everyone else reads first. Re-anchor before going technical: 'Before I take you through the architecture, I would love to understand which of the two integrations you are actually trying to solve' - that is the IT director's language, and it establishes you as a peer to him without abandoning the CEO.

options.text: Ask the IT director a question first - 'What broke last time you tried this?' - and let the CEO listen to an answer he does not know.
options.outcome: The question is excellent - it is the most revealing question in enterprise sales, and it produces the real requirements. The CEO, hearing a candid answer he could not have given, gains respect for you. Risk: if the IT director is guarded, you have just asked a question that exposes his failure in front of his boss.
options.feedback: High-value and high-risk, and the risk is real but manageable with a soft landing: 'I am trying to understand what usually goes wrong with this kind of rollout, so we do not build something that breaks your team.' That framing makes it about your risk, not their history. The follow-on discipline matters more than the question: get the answer, then ask the CEO for the constraint that matters to him, so the room leaves with both of their concerns on the table.

scenarios.coachingNote: In any room with a hierarchy, how you treat the most senior person is the first thing everyone else reads. When a senior person invites you to talk down to someone, honour the intent, keep the frame, and give the junior person a real answer. Status is not conferred by a title in the room; it is conferred by the room's observation of who you are with.

exercises.title: Circumplex Calibration: three deliveries of the same 90 seconds
exercises.instructions: Choose a 90-second update you will actually have to give this week - a project status, a metric, a decision request. Record it three times with the same words and the same content: once deliberately warm and accommodating, once deliberately dominant and clipped, once deliberately dominant and warm. Keep the script identical each time; only delivery changes. Then watch all three back to back without sound, and a second time with sound. You are looking for one thing only: which version made you want to keep talking. That is your default quadrant, and it is almost never the one you intended.
exercises.deliverable: Three recorded 90-second videos plus a one-paragraph note naming your default quadrant, its cost, and the single axis you will adjust.
successCriteria: The script content is identical across all three recordings, verifiable by transcript, so the only variable is delivery.
In the silent pass, the dominant-and-warm version is judged by an observer as the most credible, not just the most energetic.
The note correctly identifies whether the default failure is too much dominance or too much warmth, using a concrete cost such as suppressed bad news or no decision.
The note names one specific behaviour to change in the next real meeting, with a measurable trigger - for example, asking the room a question at least once every ten minutes.
exercises.liveCoachPrompt: We are going to find your default, and your default is the thing you would rather not know about. Record the same 90 seconds three times - warm and accommodating, dominant and clipped, then dominant and warm - with identical words. Watch them back silently first, because a silent replay exposes delivery that sound hides. Tell me which one made you want to keep talking. That is the version the world hears, and we are going to work out what it costs you.

exercises.title: The Room Temperature Log: ten meetings, ten reads
exercises.instructions: Over ten real meetings in the next two weeks - a standup, a 1:1, a customer call, a board or leadership meeting, a design review, a dinner conversation - keep a log. For each meeting, record: date and setting; the senior person in the room and how you identified them; the temperature at the start and at the end on the five-point scale from cold to hot; the tier-one evidence you actually observed; your diagnosis from the four causes (unclear content, missing stakes, unresolved opposition, no frame set by the senior person); and the move you took, if any. Do not change your behaviour for the first five meetings. You are establishing a baseline, and a baseline you have already altered is worthless.
exercises.deliverable: A ten-meeting log with a diagnosis and evidence per meeting, plus a summary of your three most common room temperatures and your three most common causes.
successCriteria: Ten completed entries with a specific evidence line for each, not a general impression - 'Lena took two calls during the last 8 minutes' rather than 'they were not engaged'.
The senior person in the room is identified in at least eight of ten meetings, with the cue used recorded.
Temperature changes are observed in at least four meetings where you took no action, which establishes the baseline drift rate.

The summary names your dominant failure mode - most commonly 'the room goes cold after the data section' or 'I lose the room when a senior person interrupts' - in behavioural rather than personality terms.
exercises.liveCoachPrompt: For the next two weeks, your only job is to watch, and to write down what you see before you explain it. Ten meetings, one line of evidence each - who was the senior person, what the temperature was, and what you saw that made you say so. Do not try to be better in the room while you are collecting the data, because a baseline you have already improved is no longer a baseline. We will read the log together at the end and find the pattern you cannot see from inside the meeting.

exercises.title: The 5-Minute Reset, rehearsed cold
exercises.instructions: Get a colleague or a friend to run a deliberately dead meeting at you for 12 minutes: a 40% slide presentation on a topic they find boring, with two people on their phones and no questions. At minute 12 you will be told the room has gone cold. You then run a full 5-Minute Reset in 90 seconds of real time, following all five stages, with the clock visible in the video so the timing is auditable. Record it. The second half of the exercise is the one that matters: watch the recording and count the seconds you spoke versus the seconds the room spoke. A reset where you talk for four minutes of the five has failed, regardless of how the room looked.
exercises.deliverable: A recorded 12-minute cold-room simulation with a visible clock and a completed 5-Minute Reset, plus a tally of speaking seconds versus room speaking seconds in the reset window.
successCriteria: All five stages are executed inside five minutes, with the timing visible and verifiable in the recording.
The reset question is a genuine content change - a different question type - not a check-in like 'does that make sense?'
The floor is explicitly handed to a person who has not spoken, with the handoff acknowledged out loud.
The room speaks for at least half of the reset window, measured by the tally, and the reset closes on a named decision or next move.
exercises.liveCoachPrompt: Your colleague is going to sit there looking bored, and two of them are going to be on their phones. You get twelve minutes, then I will tell you the room is cold and you will have five minutes to change it. Watch two things in yourself: the clock, because the stages have real deadlines, and your own mouth, because the most common failure is spending four of the five minutes explaining the reset rather than running it. The score is how many seconds the room talked.

exercises.title: Status Cue Audit of your own organisation
exercises.instructions: Complete the Status Cue Audit on your own company. Build the cue list by observing three real meetings and writing down, for each: who was addressed by title and who by first name, who spoke first, who was interrupted and by whom, who was asked for their view, whose laptop was open, and who was thanked. Mark each cue legitimate or game. Then audit yourself: list the three status games you personally play, with an example of each from a real meeting in the last month, and estimate the airtime each one cost. Finally, write a one-paragraph rule for what you will not do to signal rank, plus the specific behaviour that replaces it.
exercises.deliverable: A cue table from three observed meetings, a self-audit naming three personal status games with real examples and their airtime cost, and a written replacement rule.
successCriteria: The cue table is drawn from three named real meetings with at least six cues recorded per meeting, not from a general impression of company culture.
Each of the three personal status games includes a specific real example with an approximate airtime cost in seconds or minutes.
The replacement rule is behaviourally specific and testable - for example, 'no speaker is interrupted to make my point; I will wait for the pause' - not a value statement.
The audit identifies at least one cue where your organisation's formal hierarchy and its behavioural hierarchy disagree, and names where your own influence is highest as a result.
exercises.liveCoachPrompt: We are going to audit the currency your company trades in. For three real meetings, I want the raw data: who got interrupted, who got asked, who spoke first, who was thanked, who was on title. Then the harder half - your own games, with real examples and the airtime each one cost you. Almost everyone discovers they interrupt most and defer most, and that the two are the same habit wearing different clothes. Name them, and we will replace them with something that actually works.

exercises.title: The senior room: take the floor and give it back
exercises.instructions: In your next real meeting where you are not the most senior person, prepare a contribution of about 90 seconds that (a) holds a fact you can defend, (b) concedes a preference, (c) asks the question the room was already asking, and (d) names one other person's contribution. When you are interrupted - and you will be - use the re-anchor move: restate your point as a question to the interrupter and hand the frame back, without conceding the substance. Do not rehearse the interruption; that is not the skill. After the meeting, write down exactly what happened, who interrupted you, what you said in the re-anchor, and whether you held the fact. Ask the interrupter afterwards what they thought you were trying to do.
exercises.deliverable: A post-meeting debrief containing the prepared contribution, the interruption, your exact re-anchor sentence, and the interrupter's stated read of your intent.
successCriteria: The contribution contains a specific, checkable fact and a concession on a matter of preference, and both are delivered in the same 90 seconds.
The re-anchor moves the point into a question addressed to the interrupter, and the fact is not abandoned in the handover.
The interrupter's stated read of your intent matches your intent - if it does not, the re-anchor needs to be more explicit about the substance, not more deferential.
The debrief identifies your personal default under interruption: competing, retreating, or going silent, in behavioural terms.
exercises.liveCoachPrompt: Here is the drill. You have 90 seconds in a room where you are not the most senior person, and your contribution holds a fact, concedes a preference, and asks the question the room was already asking. When you get interrupted - you will - you do not compete and you do not retreat. You re-anchor: the fact stays on the table, the point becomes a question to the person who interrupted you, and you hand the frame back. Then, afterwards, you ask them what they thought you were doing. That answer is the score.

exercises.title: Reflection: which presence do you actually want to be judged on?
exercises.instructions: Write 600 words, in longhand or in a document, answering four questions. One: when someone says you have 'executive presence', what specifically do they mean, and would you accept that description? Two: which parts of your current presence are you performing rather than producing, and for whom? Three: who in your professional world is a presence model, and what does their model cost them that you would not pay? Four: what is one behaviour from the GLOBE practices - composure, warmth, integrity, trustworthiness, dynamism - that you are currently failing in a specific, observable way? End by writing the single behaviour change you will make in the next 30 days and how you will know it happened.
exercises.deliverable: A 600-word written reflection and one specific 30-day behavioural commitment with an observable indicator.
successCriteria: The reflection names the specific behaviours behind the phrase 'executive presence' rather than treating it as a personality verdict.
The second section identifies at least one performed behaviour and names the audience it is performed for.
The third section identifies a real cost borne by a real presence model, not an imagined one.
The 30-day commitment is behavioural, observable, and attached to a date and a check-in - not an intention to be more confident.
exercises.liveCoachPrompt: This one has no technique in it, and that is why it works. Four questions, 600 words, and the third one is the important one: whose presence do you admire, and what does it cost them that you would refuse to pay. The term 'executive presence' has quietly become a way of describing people who look like the people already in the room, and the most useful thing you can do with it is decide deliberately which parts of it you are actually willing to adopt. Be honest on the page - nobody else is grading this.

assessment.title: The room that disagrees
assessment.brief: You are given a live, high-stakes meeting to run: a 30-minute leadership team meeting where a scenario has been engineered so that the room is cold at the start, contains a senior person who disagrees with your proposal in public, and includes two participants who are visibly disengaged. You must run the meeting, take the disagreement, execute a 5-minute reset when the room drops, and close on a decision or a named next move with a specific owner and date. The recording is watched for both the content of your interventions and your room management, and the debrief is run against the live transcript.

rubric.excellent: Names the room's temperature early and correctly from tier-one evidence - orientation, phone use, overlap, question quality - and identifies the cause as one of the four (unclear content, missing stakes, unresolved opposition, no frame set by the senior person), with a move matched to that specific cause.
rubric.adequate: Recognises the room is disengaged and takes a reasonable remedial action, but the diagnosis is general - 'they seem bored' - and the move is a generic energy intervention rather than one targeted at the cause.
rubric.poor: Does not register the room's state at all, or notices only after a participant has visibly disengaged, and continues presenting regardless.

rubric.excellent: Holds the dominant-and-warm quadrant deliberately for the whole meeting: decisive on the decision, generous with credit, and never so dominating that the senior person shuts down or the room stops volunteering information.
rubric.adequate: Maintains control of the floor and the agenda with a broadly appropriate register, but drifts - visible over-explanation, or a noticeable softening when challenged that costs the substance.
rubric.poor: Either dominates to the point that participation collapses and no information surfaces, or accommodates so fully that no decision is made and the meeting ends without a commitment.

rubric.excellent: Holds status through preparation, specificity, and specific public attribution, and models the behaviour for the room: the senior person is not undermined, the dissent is credited before it is addressed, and no airtime is spent on status signalling.
rubric.adequate: Keeps the room's attention and does not visibly posture, though the presence of some credential or title-based framing weakens the credibility of the contributions.
rubric.poor: Performs rank in the room - interrupting, name-dropping, or defending a position by asserting authority rather than evidence - and the room visibly withdraws.

rubric.excellent: Acknowledges the objection in its strongest form, reframes the disagreement into a shared trade-off with both branches priced, moves the decision to where authority actually sits, and keeps the room working rather than watching a duel.
rubric.adequate: Handles the challenge without defensiveness and without conceding the substance, though the reframe is partial - for example, acknowledges the risk but does not put the alternative cost in front of the room.
rubric.poor: Defends at length, concedes the position, appeals to the most senior person to close the discussion, or re-litigates the challenge in a way that turns the meeting into a contest.

rubric.excellent: Runs a full 5-Minute Reset within the window: changes the question type, changes the physical state, asks one real question and holds silence, hands the floor to a participant who has not spoken, names the trade-off, and closes the reset on a decision or a named next move.
rubric.adequate: Performs a partial reset - typically a question and a change of physical state - that visibly improves engagement, but does not change the participation structure or close the loop.
rubric.poor: No reset, or the 'reset' is a check-in ('does that make sense?') that leaves the room's structure, participation, and content unchanged.

rubric.dimension: Clarity of framing and decision closure
rubric.excellent: Every intervention is tied to the decision the meeting must produce, numbers are specific and defensible, and the close names the decision, the owner, and the date with the room's agreement.
rubric.adequate: The meeting produces a reasonable outcome and the content is generally clear, but the close lacks a specific owner or date, or a key claim during the meeting was asserted without a number behind it.
rubric.poor: The meeting ends without a decision or a next move, or the discussion is conducted in abstractions and assertions that could not survive a challenge from the room.

readingList.title: The Power Paradox
readingList.author: Chris Keltner
readingList.why: The best available treatment of what power does to a person's cognition, and the strongest evidence-based argument for acquiring status through work rather than performance. Pairs directly with the Status Cue Audit framework.

readingList.title: Never Split the Difference
readingList.author: Chris Voss
readingList.why: Tactical empathy, labelling, and the treatment of 'no' as the start of negotiation - the practical mechanics for handling a room that disagrees with you without escalating. Directly supports the disagreement-handling scenarios.

readingList.title: The Fearless Organization
readingList.author: Amy C. Edmondson
readingList.why: Psychological safety as the precondition for the candour executive presence actually requires. Without it, composure and warmth are just surface, and the room withholds the information you need.

readingList.title: Group Dynamics
readingList.author: Don Forsyth
readingList.why: The textbook grounding for group norms, status structures, conformity, and influence tactics - the academic base under reading a room and the senior person in it.

readingList.title: The Third Man
readingList.author: Colin Wilson
readingList.why: A literary and philosophical treatment of the unseen third presence that a room creates, and a useful non-academic companion to the question of who is actually in the room with you.

readingList.title: Crucial Conversations
readingList.author: Patterson, Grenny, McMillan and Switzler
readingList.why: A usable model for high-stakes disagreement in rooms where the temperature has dropped - shared brain, make it safe, then state the point. A practical companion to the 5-Minute Reset.

masteryChecklist: I can define executive presence behaviourally - composure, warmth, integrity, demonstrated status - and reject both the coaching version of the term and the 7-38-55 shortcut.
I can plot my own default behaviour on the dominance and warmth axes and name the specific cost of my dominant failure mode.
I can identify the senior person in a room within ninety seconds, from interruption patterns and turn-taking, and calibrate to their frame rather than my preferred one.
I can take a public objection in a senior room, reframe it as a priced trade-off, and hand the decision back to the room without conceding the substance.
I can run a full five-minute reset in a cold room - changing the question type, the physical state, and the participation structure - and close it on a decision.
I can audit the status cues in my own organisation, name my own status games with real examples, and replace them with attribution and specificity.
I can hold authority in a room I do not outrank by conceding on preference, keeping ground on fact, and asking the question the room was already asking.
